sections.overview: The humpback whale is a baleen whale found in all major oceans. Most populations migrate between high-latitude feeding grounds and warmer breeding areas, but the Arabian Sea population remains in its region year-round. Males sing patterned songs, and South Pacific research documents song themes spreading socially between populations.
sections.identification: Adults have a stocky dark-grey body, a broad flattened head and a small dorsal fin behind the midpoint; the fin varies in shape. Females average about 15 metres and are slightly longer than males in NOAA’s Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory account. The pectoral fins reach roughly one-third of body length; fleshy tubercles on the head and lower jaw bear sensory hairs. Researchers identify individuals by the distinctive black-and-white pattern beneath each broad fluke. Adults reach about 11–16 m and 40 US tons (roughly 36 metric tonnes); females are slightly larger than males.
sections.habitat: Migratory populations typically feed in cold, productive high-latitude waters in summer and move to tropical or subtropical breeding grounds in winter. Some whales travel up to 8,000 kilometres between feeding and breeding grounds; routes differ among populations and hemispheres. Southern populations commonly breed from July to October and feed near Antarctica from November to March; northern populations follow the opposite seasonal cycle. Arabian Sea whales are resident rather than migratory, using warm regional waters that also provide feeding opportunities through seasonal upwelling.
sections.diet: Prey varies geographically: Southern Hemisphere whales mainly take Antarctic krill, while northern populations eat small schooling fish including herring, anchovies and sand lance. During a lunge, a whale engulfs prey-rich water; expandable throat grooves let the mouth and ventral pouch distend. It then expels water through fringed baleen plates that retain prey. In Southeast Alaska, solitary tagged whales formed bubble curtains around krill layers before lunging through the concentrated prey. This detailed bubble-net mechanism is documented at that Alaskan feeding site and does not establish a universal tactic.
sections.behavior: Breeding groups are fluid: a female may travel with a calf and a principal male escort, while other males join and jostle for close position. Off eastern Australia, observed males used both escorting and singing tactics; whether song attracts females or mediates competition remains debated. In Hawaiian breeding-area recordings, social “wops” and “grumbles” varied with group context and were quieter when a nearby singing whale could hear them. South Pacific recordings show song themes spreading between populations and some singers combining old and newly introduced material during rapid song change.
sections.reproduction: Mating and birth occur mainly in warm lower-latitude waters during each hemisphere’s winter; gestation lasts about 11 to 11.5 months. A pregnant female feeds on temperate or polar grounds to build reserves before returning to give birth; she may reach breeding areas before other whales. Females usually have one calf every two or three years, and mother-calf pairs often use shallow, sheltered water. Calves nurse for about 10 to 11 months; compiled estimates place their length near 4.3 metres at birth and 8.8 metres at weaning. In Exmouth Gulf, resting lactating females had respiration rates about half those of adults on feeding grounds, consistent with rest conserving maternal energy.
sections.ecology: Baleen whales release nitrogen, phosphorus and iron near the surface in waste, and these nutrients can support phytoplankton growth. A recent model including humpbacks among several whale species estimated variable regional and seasonal effects of whale nutrient recycling on primary production. The model does not isolate a global contribution attributable to humpbacks alone.
sections.conservation: NOAA reports that commercial whaling greatly reduced all humpback populations and depleted most by more than 95 percent before the commercial-whaling moratorium. An IWC assessment found strong overall North Pacific recovery from the low level around 1966, with a peak in 2014 and regional declines linked to the 2014–2016 marine heatwave. The CSG’s 2025-2 summary lists the species globally as Least Concern but the Arabian Sea and Oceania subpopulations as Endangered. The global Least Concern assessment was published in November 2018; the separate Arabian Sea assessment is dated 2008. Current pressures include entanglement in fishing gear and debris, vessel strikes and disturbance, underwater noise, and climate-related changes to prey; their effects vary by region. NOAA notes that entanglement can impair feeding or cause injury and death, while prey shifts may worsen nutritional condition and affect reproduction.
